paper_title: VAE Rhythm: Temporal Decoding Traces for AI-Generated Video Detection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visible artifacts are an unreliable cue for detecting generated videos, because newer generators learn to remove them. We instead detect a trace left by the generation pipeline itself. Most video generators decode latents with a 3D causal VAE that groups consecutive frames in time, so the fidelity of generated frames rises and falls periodically with their position in a group. We call this periodic trace VAE Rhythm. Real videos are captured frame by frame and do not have it. To reveal it without training, we propose a phase scan. The scan reconstructs a clip with an off-the-shelf VAE from successive start offsets and measures the periodicity of the reconstruction error across these offsets. We find VAE Rhythm in most of the 39 variants of 31 generators we test, including the closed-source Sora, Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0. We use the rhythm as a zero-shot score, as a plug-in for existing detectors and as a data engine that pairs real videos with their VAE reconstructions to train our detector CaDet. On DF26, the training-free rhythm score outperforms all 15 retrained baselines, and as a plug-in it improves all 19 tested detectors by 6.7% to 23.7% AUROC. CaDet achieves the best AUROC on AIGVDBench, DF26 and three 2026 closed-source models, and its variant trained without any generated video still exceeds 90% on AIGVDBench.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video generators such as Sora [55, 56], Veo [22, 80], Kling [35] and Seedance [21, 78] now produce clips that people can no longer reliably tell from camera recordings. On DF26, human viewers identify generated clips with nearchance accuracy [67]. Preference tuning [99] lets each new model remove the flicker and deformation that viewers notice, so detectors built on such visible artifacts chase moving target. durable cue should lie in the perceptual blind spot of video generation. Traces in this blind spot are invisible to humans, so developers have no reason to remove them. To find such traces, we look at how generated videos are formed. We observe that most open-source [1, 26, 36, 82] and closed-source [21, 50] video generators decode latents into frames with 3D causal VAE [59, 64, 100]. Specifically, to reduce computation, the VAE compresses time by grouping consecutive frames into shared latents. In the standard 4 Corresponding author. Figure 1: VAE Rhythm. (a) 4 causal VAE decodes frames in groups, illustrated on Sora frames. (b) As the VAE window shifts, its groups realign with those of the clip every four starts. The residual r(k) of typical Sora clip therefore oscillates, while that of typical real clip stays nearly flat. scheme of Figure 1a, the first frame is encoded alone and each later group of four frames shares one latent. This grouping is invisible to viewers, but it fixes the position of each generated frame within group. Can we detect this grouping from the pixels of video without access to its generator? To investigate this question, we reconstruct generated videos with an off-the-shelf video VAE and shift the frame at which the reconstruction starts. We find that the reconstruction error rises and falls periodically with this shift, and the period equals the group size. Because causal 3D convolutions treat the positions within group differently, the fidelity of generated frame depends on its position in its group [90]. The reconstruction error is therefore lowest whenever the groups of the two VAEs align. We call this periodic phenomenon VAE Rhythm. camera captures each frame independently, so real videos lack it. We measure VAE Rhythm with training-free phase scan, shown in Figure 1b. frozen 4 VAE reconstructs -frame window of the clip from each start offset = 0, . . . , 1. For each reconstructed frame, we subtract the mean error of that frame over all windows that contain it, 1 which removes the effect of frame content. Averaging these differences within the window gives residual r(k) for offset k. The rhythm score is the share of the variance of r(k) at the period of the rhythm. Earlier reconstruction-based detectors use the level of the error [44, 46, 63, 85], whereas the phase scan uses only its periodicity. We run the phase scan on 39 variants of 31 generators released from 2023 to 2026. The rhythm appears in both opensource and closed-source models. Figure 2 shows it in Sora, Kling 3.0, Grok Imagine [92] and Seedance 2.0. Compared with real clips, the rhythm is significantly stronger in 30 of 36 matched variants. Different generated clips also oscillate in phase. Their error minima tend to fall at the same start offsets, because every generated video starts its first group at its first frame. Real clips show no such common offset. In control experiments, VAE round trip induces the rhythm in real clips, whereas H.264 [88] re-encoding does not. VAE Rhythm is thus invisible to viewers but measurable from pixels alone, so it lies in the perceptual blind spot of video generation. We exploit it for detection in three ways. First, the rhythm score itself is zero-shot detector that needs no training. Second, the VAE Rhythm plug-in adds the rhythm score to the score of any existing detector when the rhythm is stronger than in typical real videos, so the detector needs no retraining. Third, the VAE-pair engine builds training data from real videos alone. It passes each real clip through frozen VAE and post-processes the clip and its reconstruction identically, so the two differ only by VAE decoding. We build our own detector on these pairs and call it CaDet, which stands for Cadence Detector. CaDet learns VAE decoding traces from the pairs in an artifact path and adds semantic path that never sees them. Its generator-free variant CaDetGF trains only the artifact path on real videos and pairs, so it never sees generated videos. All three uses improve detection. Without training, the zero-shot score reaches 76.2% AUROC on DF26 and beats the best of 15 retrained baselines by 5.8%. The plug-in improves all 19 tested detectors on DF26 by 6.7% to 23.7%. CaDet is best on AIGVDBench, DF26 and three 2026 closedsource models, and CaDet-GF reaches 90.9% and 91.9% on AIGVDBenchs openand closed-source generators. Our contributions are: We identify VAE Rhythm as periodic trace of temporal grouping in video VAEs and propose training-free phase scan to measure it. We analyze VAE Rhythm in 39 variants of 31 generators and show that it is common in openand closed-source models and originates in VAE decoding. We use VAE Rhythm as zero-shot score, plug-in and VAE-pair engine, and improve detection on AIGVDBench, DF26 and 2026 closed-source models.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Synthetic media and video detection. Following face and image forgery benchmarks [15, 65, 107], video benchmarks include GenVideo [11], DVF [69], GenVidBench [53], AIGVDBench [48], ViF-Bench [40], GenBuster [86, 87], CoCoVideo [19] and DF26 [67]. Image and face detectors study spatial, frequency and attention cues [20, 34, 45, 60, 71, 76, 84]. Others use domain-general, contrastive or continual learning [66, 70, 72, 74, 96], or adapt frozen vision backbones [57, 61] through intermediate features, subspaces or transferable concepts [14, 37, 43, 54, 98, 105]. Video detectors build on action-recognition backbones [5, 39, 52, 79], spatiotemporal models [3, 11, 17, 38, 41, 47, 95], trainingfree feature statistics [4, 30, 32, 102, 103] and multimodal LLMs that reason about images and videos [40, 58, 75, 77, 86, 87, 106]. Audits also document format and metadata confounds in existing benchmarks [7, 17, 23, 49, 58]. We instead measure temporal trace of VAE decoding that many generator families share. Generator-derived cues and video VAEs. Reconstruction error is an established cue for generated images [9, 16, 46, 63, 85], and diffusion models can also guide detector features [73]. Video detectors use reconstruction error [12, 44] and inversion noise [91], and concurrent work probes flow trajectories [8]. Image [9, 24, 62] and video detectors [17, 18] also train on pairs of real data and their autoencoder reconstructions, with the reconstructions labelled as generated. Video VAEs compress time with causal 3D convolutions [1, 26, 33, 36, 82, 94, 100, 101]. IV-VAE [90] reports unequal quality within frame groups, and WF-VAE [42] reduces seams between chunks. We instead measure the periodicity of reconstruction error across temporal alignments. We also build VAE pairs from real videos with shared postprocessing, so the VAE is the only difference within pair.

sections.title: 3 Understanding VAE Rhythm
sections.content: Mechanism. causal video VAE with temporal compression factor maps 1 + frames to 1 + latent steps [82, 100, 101]. It encodes the first frame separately, and each later latent step expands into group of output frames. The group boundaries at frames 1, 1 + T, 1 + 2T, . . . form temporal lattice. Causal convolutions can span several groups, but they treat the positions in this lattice differently, so reconstruction quality is unequal within group [90]. We call the resulting periodic signature VAE Rhythm. Camera acquisition has no such lattice, although codecs and framerate conversion can add their own periodic structure, which Section S1.2 in the supplement examines.

sections.title: 3.2 VAE Rhythm across generators
sections.content: Our census covers all 39 generator variants that support 24 offsets: 26 from AIGVDBench, 10 from DF26 [2, 27, 81, 89], MiniMax H3, and Seedance 2.0 and 2.5. The five 16-frame 2D-VAE variants in AIGVDBench [6, 10, 13, 25] are too short for this scan. Qualitative evidence. Figure 2 shows the mean profiles r(k) of the two real cohorts and of six generators that we selected for signal strength and prominence. Figure S1 in the supplement shows all 39 variants, including weak and negative cases. We average the profiles as measured, without phase alignment, smoothing or subtraction of the real mean. Repeated peaks and troughs survive this averaging over unrelated clips in open-source and closed-source models alike. The period is four frames in most families, eight in LTX and Kling 3.0, and about five in Wan 2.6. The real means show no repeating pattern, only late-offset excursion that the generated means share. Quantitative evidence. We compare the 36 variants with window-matched scans against the real clips of their own benchmark. sections.title: 3.3 Zero-shot detection with the rhythm
sections.content: The tests above compare groups of clips. To check whether the rhythm also separates individual clips, we use it directly as detection score without training, thresholds or calibration. We scan each clip once with the frozen Wan2.1 VAE and score it with the share of residual variance at the period of its family. This score is C4 by default, C8 for the eight-frame Kling 3.0 and LTX 2.3 T2V, and Ppk for the period-5 Wan 2.6. We measure its AUROC against the real clips of the same benchmark, where 50% is chance. Table 1 shows representative results, and Table S2 in the supplement lists all variants. The score exceeds chance on 34 of the 36 window-matched variants. As the mechanism predicts, it is strongest on open-source generators with 4 VAE. It also works on closed-source models with unknown VAEs, such as Sora and Kling 3.0. It is weaker on the 8 LTX family, because our 4 measurement VAE does not match it. Most DF26 and 2026 generators improve at 720p, which is consistent with the scale dependence. Gen-2 and Pika stay below chance, which matches their flat curves. With the single statistic Ppk for all generators, the score reaches 76.2% on DF26s ten generators. The best retrained baseline on DF26 is Effort, and the score exceeds it by 5.8%. Supervised detectors train on AIGVDBenchs own Open-Sora clips, so on AIGVDBench the score trails most of them.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Section 3 shows that VAE decoding causes the rhythm and that an off-the-shelf VAE measures it across generators. We therefore build on frozen VAE and real videos rather than on any particular generator. Figure 5 summarizes the method.

The two members share content and every random choice of the chain, so the VAE is their only difference. Many benchmarks confound generation with format and metadata [7, 23]. Within pair, format and metadata are identical, so they cannot tell the two members apart. Figure 5: Overview. (a) frozen video VAE has two uses. The periodicity of its phase scan gives the zero-shot score sc, and its round trip creates the VAE pairs, which differ only by VAE decoding. (b) On one frozen DINOv3 backbone, CaDet trains an artifact path with the pairs and semantic path without them. The chain mimics the processing of online videos. It trims few leading frames and rescales the clip to common delivery size. It may also interpolate, duplicate or drop frames before it re-encodes the clip with x264 or x265 at random quality. Section S4 in the supplement gives the parameters. Both members share the chain, so the detector learns VAE traces that survive this processing. Processing alone also never signals generation. Each pair draws its VAE from three 4 VAEs and one 8 VAE, so the detector learns traces that several VAEs share. Following the scale law in Section S1.6 of the supplement, we sample over several scales and let the chain upscale some clips.

sections.title: 4.2 CaDet: two paths on one frozen backbone
sections.content: Decoding traces may weaken or change when closed-source generator uses an unknown VAE and post-processing, so cues that do not depend on the VAE are also needed. Section 5.4 shows that one model does not easily learn both, because adding the VAE pairs to Effort [98] hurts it on closedsource generators. CaDet therefore attaches two paths to one frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 [68]. The artifact path learns decoding traces from the pairs, and the semantic path never sees them. Freezing the backbone keeps its pretrained features and is meant to limit overfitting. Both paths share the frozen weights, so CaDet stores one backbone and two small trainable parts. Artifact path. LoRA [29] adapters on the attention projections feed two heads. The generic head reads the final class token and is trained with counterfactual labels. Both members of every pair count as real, and only generator-produced clips count as generated. Section S3 in the supplement shows that VAE reconstructions are smoother and less noisy than their sources. head that calls them generated may learn that smoothness means generation and then miss sharp closedsource videos. The counterfactual labels make this appearance useless to the generic head. The artifact head reads class-token and patch-token statistics of intermediate layers because we expect these layers to keep more low-level detail. It keeps the original labels to learn the decoding traces, and its gradient also updates the shared adapters. The path score sums the two head scores after standardizing each on real videos. Table S5 in the supplement supports the two heads and the shared gradient. Semantic path. Following Effort [98], this path freezes the principal singular subspace of every attention matrix and trains only the smallest singular component and linear head. Effort argues that the frozen subspace preserves pretrained knowledge and that the small trainable part limits overfitting. The path trains frame by frame, and clips score is the logit of its mean frame probability. Fusion and the generator-free variant. At test time, we standardize the score of each path by its mean and standard deviation on held-out real clips and sum the two to obtain sd. Both terms then count standard deviations above typical real videos, so we add them without fitting any weight on generated videos. CaDet-GF trains only on real videos and their pairs. sections.title: 4.3 The VAE Rhythm plug-in
sections.content: CaDet averages frame-level evidence over time, and most other detectors also do not measure temporal periodicity explicitly. The plug-in therefore adds the training-free rhythm score sc to the score sd of any detector, including CaDet, without retraining it. We use sc = Ppk of Section 3.1 because it assumes no period and thus also covers the period of five frames that conversion from 24 to 30 fps creates. Let z() be standardization computed on real videos only. The plug-in score is = z(sd) + max (cid:0)0, z(sc)(cid:1). (3) After z() both scores measure how far clip lies above typical real videos. They can therefore be added without fitting any parameter on generated videos. The rhythm score is continuous, so z(sc) subtracts its mean over real videos and divides by its standard deviation. Detector scores are often saturated probabilities, and most real-video scores are below 103. Inside the range of the real-video scores, z(sd) therefore maps score to the standard-normal quantile of its mid-rank position among them. Beyond that range it continues linearly with slope 1/σ, where σ is the standard deviation of the real-video scores. The detector thus keeps its ordering of the clips that score above every real video. strong rhythm is evidence of generation. weak rhythm is not evidence of authenticity, because static scenes and post-processing can also weaken it. The positive part therefore only adds evidence, and Section 5.4 shows that it limits losses where the rhythm is weak. For clip whose rhythm is at or below the real mean, the fused score equals z(sd), so the detector decides alone. We scan each clip at native resolution and downscale only short sides above 720 pixels, because rhythm strength depends on the scan scale. Both standardizations use held-out real videos scanned in the same way, and all test sets share them.

sections.content: Protocol. We follow the one-to-all protocol of AIGVDBench [48]. Detectors train on 14,000 Open-Sora [104] clips and 14,000 OpenVid [51] real clips and are tested on 20 open-source and 11 closed-source generators against 3,000 real clips. We average the per-generator AUROC over open-source, unseen open-source and closed-source generators. Without retraining, we also evaluate on DF26 [67], which has ten generators released in 2025 and 2026 and permits content-paired 2AFC evaluation. The 2026 models are single-shot clips of MiniMax H3, Seedance 2.5 [83] and Seedance 2.0 [28], compared against the DF26 reals. We also test on ViF-Bench [40], and Section S6 in the supplement lists all test-set sizes. All detectors use the same 8 frames from shared 2562 cache, followed by method-specific input transforms. No test clip enters detector training or the engine. The engine uses the VAEs of Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo, CogVideoX and LTX-Video [26, 36, 82, 100]. sections.title: 5.2 Main results
sections.content: On AIGVDBench, CaDet reaches 93.9% AUROC on opensource and 95.8% on closed-source generators. The strongest reproduced baselines there are ForgeLens and Effort, and CaDet exceeds them by 8.2% and 3.3%. Without generatorproduced training clips, CaDet-GF still reaches 90.9% and 91.9%. This is well above the same backbone trained on Open-Sora without pairs, so the pairs carry most of the performance here. CaDet also leads on the 2026 closed-source models and on all four DF26 averages. Its DF26 all-generator AUROC of 78.5% beats Effort by 8.1%. Table S4 in the supplement reports each newer generator. Over the four closed-source generators of DF26 and the three 2026 models, CaDet averages 83.0% and exceeds the strongest baseline TimeSformer by 2.6%. Among the 2026 models, CaDet exceeds Effort by 17% on Seedance 2.5. On Kling 3.0 and on the Wan 2.2 and HunyuanVideo 1.5 generators of DF26, the training-free scan alone matches or exceeds every detector in Table S4. All methods perform poorly on ViF-Bench because its reals are re-encoded to 256p at 16 fps.

Following Section S2 in the supplement, their open-source average covers the 15 generators whose scans match the real clips, so the base scores differ slightly from Table 2. Across 39 generators, the gain averaged over detectors follows the zero-shot AUROC of the rhythm with = 0.89 and turns positive once that AUROC passes about 55%. The plug-in therefore helps where rhythm is measurable and changes little elsewhere. This explains the smaller effect on AIGVDBenchs closedsource generators and the 2026 models, where the rhythm is weaker. On these two groups, 13 and 18 of the 19 detectors still improve. sections.title: 5.4 Ablations
sections.content: Tables 4 and 5 separate the contributions of the rhythm evidence, the VAE pairs and the two paths. Table S5 in the supplement adds leave-one-VAE-out and other variants. Rhythm evidence. The signal comes from periodicity, not from the size of the reconstruction error. If lower error is treated as generated, the error falls below chance on DF26, whereas periodicity is 34.4% higher. Excluding the first window frame and subtracting the frame baseline both help on DF26 and the 2026 models. As plug-in evidence, only periodicity helps. The reconstruction error and the scores of another weak detector both lower CaDet on DF26, whereas periodicity raises it. The positive part limits losses on AIGVDBench and the 2026 models, where the rhythm is weak. VAE pairs. On one backbone, post-processed real clips alone help on closed-source generators, which suggests less reliance on processing artifacts. Adding the VAE reconstructions raises the open-source AUROC by 19.2%. Leaving out any one of the four VAEs keeps it between 89.1% and 93.4%, so the engine does not rely on single VAE. On DF26s closed-source generators, however, the pairs lower both this backbone and Effort. The semantic path therefore omits them, so that CaDet keeps both strengths. Two paths. Figure 6c shows that the two paths succeed on different generators. On the 43 unseen generators, their AUROCs barely correlate, with = 0.30. The artifact path is better on 19 of the 25 open-source generators, which fits the pairs teaching decoding artifacts. The semantic path is better on all four closed-source models of DF26. Their sum beats the better path on 21 of 43 generators and is never below their average. This is not generic ensemble effect. We sample 100 real clips and 15 clips of each DF26 generator and keep their first 2.5 s. Re-compression uses x264 at CRF 23 to 38. Downscaling reduces the short side from 720 to 540 or 360 pixels, and interpolation raises the frame rate by 1.25 or 2 times. The rhythm score changes little at CRF 28 and stays above chance after downscaling and frame interpolation. The plug-in therefore keeps adding evidence after processing, and it raises TimeSformer under every setting. With the plug-in, CaDet remains the strongest detector under frame interpolation and under moderate compression or downscaling. Under the strongest settings, it is on par with TimeSformer with the plug-in. Section S6 in the supplement gives the settings.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: We identify VAE Rhythm as hidden temporal signature of frame grouping in 3D causal video VAEs. Across 39 scannable generator variants, training-free phase scan finds it in openand closed-source families, and controls and scale law support its origin in decoding. Pairs built from real videos enable generator-free detection, semantic path makes our detector the strongest in our comparison, and the plug-in improves every tested detector on DF26. Because the rhythm comes from decoding rather than from content, it complements detectors that learn appearance, and the plug-in adds it to them without any training. Like other pixel-level traces, the rhythm needs some motion and scan scale close to the generation scale, and strong re-encoding or frame-rate conversion can weaken it. Future generators may also change their VAEs. The engine needs only real videos and VAE, so new VAE can be added to training without collecting any generated video.

They cover the full atlas of all 39 variants in Figure S1, pervariant statistics, controls, the zero-shot census, phase and spectral summaries, family-dependent periods, the scale law and the choice of measurement VAE. Figure S1 plots every available 24-offset profile in the census subsets at native resolution capped at 480p. The profiles have no phase alignment, smoothing, per-video amplitude normalization or real-reference subtraction. Vertical ranges start at 4% and expand by powers of two as needed, and each panel labels its limits. The bottom row has no real overlays, because the newer collections lack their own real cohort and the short-window scans lack matched = 9 reference. HunyuanVideo appears under both window settings. The five 16-frame 2D-VAE variants cannot support 24 offsets and are omitted. S1.1 Per-variant statistics Table S1 lists the values behind Figure 3. S1.4 Phase, spectrum and barcode summaries Figure S2 includes HunyuanVideo 1.5, LTX 2.3, Wan 2.6, Seedance 2.5 and the 480p and 720p scans of Grok and Veo 3.1. It typically samples up to 100 clips per generator. The codec controls use 120 real clips, and the amplitude ratio uses the median amplitude relative to AIGVDBench reals. These summaries use sampled clips and the real-reference correction. They complement the raw profiles of the full collections in Figure S1, and their sample counts and processing differ. Figure 4 stacks the corrected residual curves by generator, with one clip per row sorted by periodicity and up to 100 clips per group. The displayed latent generators show aligned bands at period 4. The bands are at period 8 for Kling 3.0 and LTX 2.3 and at period 5 for Wan 2.6, whereas real clips lack comparable pattern. Figure S4 summarizes the dominant periods from 256p scan with K=60 of closed-source clips in AIGVDBench, GenBuster and ViF-Bench. The period-4 share is 68% for Sora against 37% for real clips, and 83% for ViF kling-v1 against 54%. S1.5 Family-dependent periods Four-frame oscillations are prominent in several 4-VAE families in Figure S1. The curves also contain longer-period structure, as in Kling 3.0 and Pyramid-Flow. LTX can contain both an eight-frame component and its four-frame harmonic. Wan 2.6 instead shows pattern of about five frames, which is consistent with change from 24 to 30 fps delivery. These differences motivate the period-independent statistic Ppk instead of test restricted to period 4. The phase distributions and spectra in Figures S2 and S3 provide complementary summaries. Unlike the raw profiles in Figure S1, they use the real-reference correction described in Section S2. S1.6 The scale law As Figure S5 shows, rhythm strength depends strongly on the ratio ρ = Rscan/G of scan resolution to generation resolution. We reconstruct real clips at short side and scan them at 256p. Their median C4 falls from 0.64 at ρ = 1 to 0.33 at ρ = 0.53 and approaches the real-video level of 0.18 at ρ = 0.36. Upscaling before scanning does not recover information lost at generation, and cropping is not equivalent to changing this ratio. Native-resolution scans capped at 480p improve the zero-shot AUROC over 256p scans. Sora rises from 72% to 90%, Luma from 62% to 79% and Wan2.1 from 79% to 99.5%. Scanning at 720p raises most DF26 and 2026 generators further, as Table S2 lists. The same scale dependence motivates the range of reconstruction resolutions that the engine uses in Section 4.1. The Wan2.1 VAE detects rhythm in videos from CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Pyramid-Flow, Grok and Seedance, and the CogVideoX VAE gives comparable results. The HunyuanVideo and LTX VAEs transfer less well, so we measure with the Wan2.1 VAE. On Kling 3.0, it gives 87% AUROC, against 57% with the 8 LTX VAE. Duplicate-frame conversion is applied with probability 0.25 and excludes interpolation. Decimation to 16 fps is applied with probability 0.3 when applicable. In duplication mode, both members first share source decimated to 815 fps. Only the generated member undergoes the VAE round trip, and both members are returned to 24 or 30 fps by repetition. The encoding parameters are also shared. The codec is x264 or x265 with equal probability, CRF is uniform in [18, 28], the number of B-frames is uniform in [0, 8], B-pyramid is enabled with probability 0.5, and the GOP length is uniform in [12, 250]. About 58% of pairs undergo interpolation, duplication or decimation. These operations can weaken pixel-domain periodicity, and the frame-level detector of Section 4.2 learns the spatial decoding traces that remain. S5 Baseline reproduction All baselines use the same 14,000 real and 14,000 Open-Sora training clips. They also use the same 8 cached frames per clip at indices 0, 4, . . . , 28 of 2562 JPEG cache at quality 95. The five 16-frame generators are AnimateDiff-T2V [25], SVD-I2V [6], SEINE-I2V [13] and both VideoCrafter [10] variants, and they use frames 0, 2, . . . , 14. An earlier version of the cache repeated their last frame, and all reported results use the corrected cache except the row marked in Table S5. We keep method-specific augmentation, optimizers and schedules where they are compatible with the protocol. We report the final checkpoint to avoid selection on in-domain validation scores, which are often saturated. Official implementations are used throughout. We adapted the protocol as follows. Effort is trained with its released DeepfakeBench code, unchanged except for the data lists. For DeMamba, fixed frames replace random temporal starts, and batch size 128 is implemented with 32 4 gradient accumulation. Its X-CLIP [52] vision tower is loaded from the full pretrained X-CLIP model. For ReStraV, the common 8-frame sequence replaces the official 24-frame trajectory at 12 fps. This gives 7 steps and 6 turning angles. CNNSpot, Gram-Net and NPR are evaluated on full 2562 frames, following their official test commands. The clip score of NPR is the logit of the mean frame probability computed in double precision, as Section S7 explains. UnivFD uses the AIGCDetectBenchmark settings with batch size 64 and augmentation probability 0.1. AIGVDBench defines ForgeLens setting 1 as training on small dataset for more epochs. We report this setting and also the same schedule on the full training set. Both ForgeLens settings use fp32 inference to avoid tied scores from autocast. TimeSformer and UniFormerV2 use the official MMAction2 Kinetics-400 configurations with two output classes and 50-epoch upper limit, so the cosine phase of UniFormerV2 is compressed to 45 epochs. NativeScale [41] fine-tunes its Qwen2.5-VL vision encoder with the official training script and the learning rate of 105 from its paper. The released step schedule would lower this rate to 106 from the first step. These changes can affect performance, especially the change in temporal sampling, and they are part of the comparison protocol. Reproduction gaps vary by method and generator split. On closed-source generators, ForgeLens setting 3 spans 75.8% to 87.1% across seeds, against the reported 76.9%. Over three seeds, Effort reaches 84.3% and 92.5% on opensource and closed-source generators, compared with the reported 87.5% and 94.1%. We keep the code revisions and per-video scores of each run.
